6372 Using Bayesian Network to Classify the Level of Service in Bus Route
Authors: I. Aljamea, A. S. Abu Zaid, M. A. Obeidat
Abstract:This paper presents using Bayesian networks for classification of the level of service in public bus route. Bus route operation level of service is an important measure of the public transportation performance, where it reflects the performance of the bus stops in the route. A new Bayesian classification approach is proposed and evaluated on collected bus route data. Evaluation is performed by comparing with support vector machine and decision tree classifiers. The experimental results show the superiority of the Bayesian networks over support vector machines and decision tree classifiers in terms of classification accuracy, F1 value, and the Bayesian network parameters.

1 Introduction
Since the pioneering work of L.E. Ballentine in Ref. , quantum coherence has been recognized as an intrinsic aspect of the quantum world. This quantum property has been extensively investigated over the past several years, since it plays a crucial role in the quantum communication and quantum information processing applications , and it has been demonstrated as an important resource in the context of quantum metrology . In general, quantum coherence is a phenomenon that can be described by the off-diagonal elements of a density matrix. However, quantum coherence can also be quantified by the diagonal elements of a density matrix [4, 5], known as quantum discord. Although it has been proven that quantum coherence and quantum discord are equivalent in some specific cases [4, 6, 7], they are fundamentally distinct quantities in general cases. Therefore, both quantum coherence and quantum discord have their specific operational advantages and disadvantages, and thus they have been widely studied in different types of quantum systems.
Recently, the concept of quantum coherence has been applied to the field of quantum information. In Ref. , the coherence of quantum channels was investigated, and it was demonstrated that coherence is a resource that can be transformed from one quantum channel to another by unitary operations in some cases. In Ref. , it is shown that the relative entropy of coherence quantifies the usefulness of coherence to perform a particular quantum computation. In Ref. , the role of coherence in the operation of the quantum eraser was discussed, and it is shown that quantum coherence is a necessary and sufficient condition for a successful quantum eraser. Recently, quantum coherence has also been applied to the field of quantum cryptography and it has been shown that quantum coherence can be effectively used as a resource for secure quantum communication .

Abstract:
A number of studies have implicated abnormal immune responses and inflammation in the pathogenesis of autism. However, little is known about the molecular basis of this association. Recent studies have identified genes and signaling pathways that are frequently deleted or mutated in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Among these genes is the kinase gene AKT3 which is deleted in a subset of individuals with ASD. The protein kinase AKT plays a critical role in promoting cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, survival and migration. To understand the role of AKT in ASD, we examined the impact of AKT loss on various properties of neural cells. Our results show that AKT activity is significantly lower in autism patient samples. We also demonstrate that reduction of AKT3 function in neuronal precursors results in abnormal neuronal development and a change in neuronal morphology and gene expression. Using a novel lentiviral vector system to knockdown AKT expression in neural cells, we have also found that AKT deletion results in enhanced dendritic spines. Together these studies suggest that AKT is important for proper neuronal development and that AKT3 loss could be a major factor in the neuropathology of ASD.

Introduction
To obtain numerical solutions for water waves, there are several different models available depending on various approximations, such as linearization, deep-water and shallow-water assumptions and numerical schemes used. It is important to select an appropriate model based on the requirements for the study. Therefore, to describe nonlinear and weakly dispersive waves with nonbreaking conditions, the depth-integrated model is a good choice. However, in the case of breaking waves, the depth-integrated model cannot be used because it is unable to describe the wave breaking. For the application to such a case, another numerical model, which can calculate wave propagation through the surf zone, must be employed. In this paper we introduce two different numerical models, the unified depth-integrated wave model (Mitsuyasu et al. 2005) and a wave breaking model based on the Reynolds Averaged Navier-Stokes equations (Mitsuyasu et al. 1999), and then present their applications to problems concerning water waves.

2382 Sparse Recovery of Non-Stationary Space–Time Signals
Authors: F. Elvadj, L. Saissonie
Abstract:We consider the recovery of space–time signals x ∈ RNM obtained by the sampling of a continuou space–time signal using a sampling operator S. More precisely, we suppose that x is a superposition of non-overlapping (in time) shifts of a single-pulse (Gaussian-like) function, and each pulse is possibly different from one channel to another. The goal is to reconstruct the space–time signal x from its partial knowledge through a recovery operator Rx defined on an oversampled space–time signal. In this paper, we consider the case where the oversampling operator S is a sampling operator in both time and space channels, and the partial knowledge of space–time signal x is taken through its discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT). We also consider the case where the oversampling operator S is a sampling operator in time channel only, and the partial knowledge of space–time signal x is given through a noisy measurement signal. Under some assumptions on the distribution of the shifts in space–time, we derive an upper bound for the recovery error, and propose a reconstruction algorithm to obtain the initial signal x.

Introduction
In Western societies, cultural traditions such as family values, beliefs, and mores have been passed down from generation to generation through various means, such as parents’ interaction with children, socialization processes, and education. Although traditions are not necessarily synonymous with values, values generally serve as the basis of traditions and are rooted in family and community norms and beliefs. Some traditions and values are more readily accepted than others, largely because of differences in the way they are taught or experienced by the various generations that live together. Some values are seen by some as more important than others and often may become the basis for arguments and conflicts among family members.
Family values and traditions can be either positive or negative depending on the family and the context. It would be rare to find a family or cultural group in which all traditions and values have been positive or negative. Some negative family traditions may have come from a positive basis, such as punishment, which may be taught as a means to discipline and/or teach behavior. This type of discipline can be positive or negative, depending on the manner in which it is implemented. For example, punishment that is not designed to help a child learn a particular behavior may be negative, while punishment that is designed to help a child learn and that includes some form of teaching may be positive. A more detailed explanation of positive and negative family traditions follows.
According to a survey conducted by Harris Interactive, 79 percent of Americans agree that traditional family values are being replaced by other values and beliefs. The respondents said that the number one factor for the loss of traditional family values was the decline of “religion,” which is commonly referred to as the erosion of family religion, and a decline in religious practices. The second most frequently cited factor was the introduction of technology and television, which were ranked as the second most frequently cited reason, followed by a decline in religious practices (Harris Interactive 2002).

Abstract:The study of stress analysis in a composite structure by using finite element method was presented in this paper. The structure of analysis was a truss that has six sections which were made of three metals (steel, magnesium, aluminum) and three composite materials (carbon fiber with epoxy resin, carbon fiber with magnesium, carbon fiber with aluminum) in the three axis directions of the truss. The stress analysis of the six sections in the same truss was analyzed and obtained and compared by using finite element method and three-dimensional elastic model of composite material.

Objectives: We investigated the frequency, patient characteristics, and clinical outcomes in patients treated with AMM for ICAD in our tertiary-care facility between 2009 and 2014. Methods: This retrospective study analyzed medical records of 526 patients with ICAD treated at our institution between 2009 and 2014. The patients were analyzed in two time periods: before (pre-) and after (post-) 2011, in which the SAMMPRIS trial results were published. AMM treatment was defined as dual antiplatelet therapy (≥ 300 mg clopidogrel daily) and intensive statin treatment (≥ 20 mg/d), for both symptomatic patients and asymptomatic patients with a recent acute ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), defined by a National Institutes of Health stroke score ≥ 4. A composite end point consisting of stroke (intracranial or extracranial), death (intracranial or extracranial), or revascularization was used as the primary outcome. Results: AMM therapy was used in 177 (33.7%) patients with symptomatic disease and in 123 (27.5%) asymptomatic patients.
